title: Book 2, Chapter 7 — Second Year of the War—The Plague of Athens—Position and Policy of Pericles—Fall of Potidæa
paragraphs: That was the funeral held during this winter, and with it the first year of the war ended. In the first days of summer the Lacedaemonians and their allies, with two-thirds of their forces as before, invaded Attica under Archidamus, son of Zeuxidamus, King of Lacedaemon. They settled in and laid waste the country. A few days after their arrival the plague first showed itself among the Athenians. It was said to have broken out earlier in many places, around Lemnos and elsewhere, but nowhere was a pestilence of such extent and deadliness remembered. At first the physicians were of no use, since they did not know how to treat it; they themselves died in the greatest numbers, because they visited the sick most often. No other human skill did any better. Supplications in the temples, divinations and the like proved equally futile, until the overwhelming force of the disaster put an end to them altogether.

The plague is said to have begun in the parts of Ethiopia above Egypt, and from there to have spread down into Egypt and Libya and most of the King’s country. It fell on Athens suddenly. It struck first at the people in Piraeus — which led them to say that the Peloponnesians had poisoned the reservoirs, there being no wells there yet — and afterwards it appeared in the upper city, where the deaths became far more frequent. As to its origin, and the causes that could be adequate to produce so great an upheaval, I leave all speculation to other writers, whether laymen or professionals. For my part, I will simply describe what it was like and set out the symptoms by which a student might perhaps recognize it, should it ever break out again. I am the better able to do this because I had the disease myself and saw others suffer from it.

That year, by general admission, was otherwise unprecedentedly free from sickness, and the few ordinary cases that did occur all ended in this disease. As a rule, however, there was no visible cause. People in good health were suddenly seized by violent heats in the head, with redness and inflammation of the eyes. The inward parts, such as the throat and tongue, turned bloody and gave off an unnatural, foul breath. Sneezing and hoarseness followed, and soon the pain reached the chest and brought on a hard cough. When it settled in the stomach, it upset it, and there came discharges of bile of every kind that physicians have named, with very great distress. In most cases an ineffectual retching followed, causing violent spasms; in some these ended soon afterward, in others much later. Outwardly the body was not very hot to the touch, nor pale, but reddish and livid, breaking out in small pustules and ulcers. Inwardly, though, it burned so fiercely that the patients could not bear to have even the lightest clothing or linen on them, and would rather be stark naked. What they wanted most was to throw themselves into cold water. Some of the neglected sick did so, plunging into the rain-tanks in their agony of unquenchable thirst; but it made no difference whether they drank little or much. On top of this, the wretched feeling of being unable to rest or sleep tormented them without ceasing. While the disease was at its height the body did not waste away, but withstood its ravages remarkably well. So when most patients died, on the seventh or eighth day, of the inward burning, they still had some strength left. But if they got past that stage and the disease descended further into the bowels, causing violent ulceration there with severe diarrhea, the resulting weakness was generally fatal. The disorder began in the head, ran its course from there through the whole body, and even where it did not kill, it left its mark on the extremities. It settled in the privy parts, the fingers and the toes, and many escaped with the loss of these, some also with the loss of their eyes. Others, on first recovering, were seized by a total loss of memory and knew neither themselves nor their friends.

The nature of the distemper was beyond all description, and its attacks were almost too grievous for human nature to endure. But it showed most clearly how different it was from all ordinary disorders in the following circumstance. All the birds and beasts that prey on human bodies either would not touch them, though many lay unburied, or died after tasting them. As proof of this, it was noticed that birds of this kind actually disappeared; they were neither near the bodies nor to be seen anywhere. But of course the effects I have mentioned could best be observed in a domestic animal like the dog.

Such, then, setting aside the many peculiar variations from case to case, were the general features of the distemper. Meanwhile the city was free of all the usual disorders, or if any case occurred, it ended in this. Some died neglected, others in the midst of every attention. No remedy was found that could be used as a specific, for what helped in one case harmed in another. Strong and weak constitutions proved equally unable to resist; all alike were swept away, even those who were dieted with the utmost care. By far the most terrible feature of the malady was the dejection that came over anyone who felt himself sickening. The despair into which they instantly fell took away their power of resistance and made them a much easier prey to the disease. Besides this, there was the awful sight of men dying like sheep after catching the infection from nursing one another. This caused the greatest mortality. If they were afraid to visit one another, they perished from neglect; indeed many houses were emptied of their inmates for lack of a nurse. If, on the other hand, they ventured to visit, death was the result. This was especially so with those who made any claim to goodness. Honor made them spare themselves nothing in attending their friends in their houses, where even the members of the family were at last worn out by the moans of the dying and gave way to the force of the disaster. Yet it was those who had recovered from the disease who showed most compassion to the sick and the dying. They knew what it was from experience and now had no fear for themselves, for the same man was never attacked twice — never at least fatally. Such persons not only received the congratulations of others but, in the elation of the moment, half entertained the vain hope that they were safe from any disease whatsoever in the future.

The existing calamity was made worse by the influx from the country into the city, and the new arrivals suffered most from it. There were no houses to receive them, so in the hot season of the year they had to be lodged in stifling cabins, where the mortality raged without restraint. The bodies of dying men lay one on top of another, and half-dead creatures reeled about the streets and crowded around all the fountains in their longing for water. The sacred places where they had quartered themselves were full of the corpses of those who had died there, just as they were. For as the disaster passed all bounds, men, not knowing what was to become of them, grew utterly careless of everything, sacred or profane. All the burial rites formerly in use were thrown into confusion, and they buried the dead as best they could. Many, lacking the proper means because so many of their friends had already died, resorted to the most shameless burials. Sometimes they got ahead of those who had built a pyre, threw their own dead on the stranger’s pyre and set it alight. Sometimes they tossed the corpse they were carrying onto another that was already burning, and went away.

Nor was this the only form of lawless extravagance that began with the plague. Men now coolly dared to do openly what they had formerly done in secret, and not simply as they pleased. They saw how quickly fortunes changed, as the prosperous suddenly died and those who had owned nothing inherited their property. So they resolved to spend quickly and enjoy themselves, regarding their lives and their riches alike as things of a day. No one was willing to persevere in what men called honor, since it was so uncertain whether they would live to attain it. It was settled that present enjoyment, and everything that contributed to it, was both honorable and useful. Neither fear of the gods nor law of man restrained them. As for the gods, they judged it made no difference whether they worshipped them or not, since they saw all alike perishing. As for the laws, no one expected to live to be brought to trial for his offenses. Each felt that a far severer sentence had already been passed on them all and hung over their heads, and that before it fell it was only reasonable to enjoy life a little.

Such was the calamity, and it weighed heavily on the Athenians, with death raging inside the city and devastation outside it. In their distress they remembered, very naturally, among other things the following verse, which the old men said had been uttered long ago:
A Dorian war shall come and with it death.

A dispute arose over whether the word in the verse had been dearth and not death. At the present juncture, of course, it was decided in favor of death, for people made their recollection fit their sufferings. I fancy, however, that if another Dorian war should ever come upon us afterwards and a dearth should happen to accompany it, the verse will probably be read accordingly. Those who knew of it also remembered now the oracle given to the Lacedaemonians. When the god was asked whether they should go to war, he answered that if they put their might into it, victory would be theirs, and that he would himself be with them. Events were thought to agree with this oracle. For the plague broke out as soon as the Peloponnesians invaded Attica. It never entered Peloponnese, at least not to an extent worth noticing, and did its worst ravages at Athens and, after Athens, in the most populous of the other towns. Such was the history of the plague.

After ravaging the plain, the Peloponnesians advanced into the Paralian region as far as Laurium, where the Athenian silver mines are. They laid waste first the side facing Peloponnese and then the side facing Euboea and Andros. But Pericles, who was still general, held the same opinion as in the previous invasion and would not let the Athenians march out against them.

While they were still in the plain, however, before they had entered the Paralian land, he had prepared an armament of a hundred ships for Peloponnese, and when all was ready he put out to sea. He took on board four thousand Athenian heavy infantry and three hundred cavalry in horse transports, which were then for the first time made out of old galleys. Fifty Chian and Lesbian vessels also joined the expedition. When this Athenian armament put out to sea, it left the Peloponnesians in Attica, in the Paralian region. At Epidaurus in Peloponnese the Athenians ravaged most of the territory and even hoped to take the town by assault, but in this they did not succeed. Leaving Epidaurus, they laid waste the territory of Troezen, Halieis and Hermione, all towns on the coast of Peloponnese. From there they sailed to Prasiai, a maritime town in Laconia, ravaged part of its territory, and took and sacked the place itself. After this they returned home, but found that the Peloponnesians had left and were no longer in Attica.

During the whole time that the Peloponnesians were in Attica and the Athenians away on the expedition in their ships, men kept dying of the plague both in the armament and in Athens. It was even asserted that the Peloponnesians hastened their departure for fear of the disorder, because they heard from deserters that it was in the city and could also see the burials going on. Yet in this invasion they stayed longer than in any other and ravaged the whole country, for they were about forty days in Attica.

The same summer Hagnon, son of Nicias, and Cleopompus, son of Clinias, the colleagues of Pericles, took the armament he had lately used and went off on an expedition against the Chalcidians in the direction of Thrace, and against Potidæa, which was still under siege. As soon as they arrived, they brought up their engines against Potidæa and tried every means of taking it. They succeeded neither in capturing the city nor in doing anything else worthy of their preparations. For the plague attacked them here also and committed such havoc that it crippled them completely. Even the soldiers of the former expedition, who had previously been healthy, caught the infection from Hagnon’s troops. Phormio and the sixteen hundred men under his command escaped only because they were no longer in the neighborhood of the Chalcidians. The end of it was that Hagnon returned with his ships to Athens, having lost one thousand and fifty out of four thousand heavy infantry in about forty days. The soldiers stationed there before remained in the country and carried on the siege of Potidæa.

After the second invasion of the Peloponnesians a change came over the spirit of the Athenians. Their land had now been laid waste twice, and war and pestilence pressed heavily on them at once. They began to find fault with Pericles as the author of the war and the cause of all their misfortunes. They became eager to come to terms with Lacedaemon and even sent ambassadors there, who did not, however, succeed in their mission. Their despair was now complete, and all of it was vented on Pericles. He saw them exasperated at the present turn of affairs and acting exactly as he had anticipated. So he called an assembly, being (it must be remembered) still general, with the double object of restoring their confidence and leading them out of these angry feelings into a calmer and more hopeful state of mind. He came forward and spoke as follows:

“I was not unprepared for the indignation you have shown toward me, for I know its causes. I have called this assembly to remind you of certain points, and to protest against your being unreasonably irritated with me or cowed by your sufferings. I hold that the greatness of the nation is of more advantage to private citizens than any individual well-being joined with public humiliation. A man may be personally as well off as you like, yet if his country is ruined he must be ruined with it; whereas a flourishing commonwealth always offers chances of salvation to unfortunate individuals. Since a state can support the misfortunes of private citizens, while they cannot support hers, it is surely the duty of everyone to be forward in her defense. It is not the duty of anyone to be, as you are, so confounded by his domestic afflictions that he gives up all thought of the common safety, and blames me for having counseled war and himself for having voted for it. And yet if you are angry with me, it is with a man who, I believe, is second to none in knowing the proper policy and in being able to expound it, and who is, moreover, not only a patriot but an honest one. A man who has that knowledge without the faculty of exposition might as well have no idea on the matter at all. If he had both gifts but no love for his country, he would be only a cold advocate of her interests. And if his patriotism were not proof against bribery, everything would go for a price. So if you thought, when you took my advice and went to war, that I was even moderately distinguished for these qualities, there is certainly no reason now why I should be charged with having done wrong.

“For those who have a free choice in the matter and whose fortunes are not at stake, war is of course the greatest of follies. But suppose the only choice was between submission with loss of independence and danger with the hope of preserving that independence. In that case it is the man who will not accept the risk who deserves blame, not the man who will. I am the same man and do not change; it is you who change. You took my advice while you were unhurt, and waited for misfortune to repent of it. The apparent error of my policy lies in the weakness of your resolution: the suffering it entails is being felt by every one of you, while its advantage is still remote and obscure to all, and a great and sudden reverse has befallen you, so that your minds are too depressed to persevere in your resolves. For the spirit quails before what is sudden, unexpected and least within calculation; and, putting all else aside, the plague has certainly been an emergency of this kind. Yet you are citizens of a great state, and you were brought up with habits equal to your birth. You should be ready to face the greatest disasters and still keep the luster of your name unimpaired. For the judgment of mankind is as relentless toward the weakness that falls short of a recognized renown as it is jealous of the arrogance that aspires higher than its due. So cease to grieve for your private afflictions, and turn instead to the safety of the commonwealth.

“If you shrink from the exertions that the war makes necessary, and fear that after all they may not have a happy result, you know the reasons by which I have often shown you that your apprehensions are groundless. If those are not enough, I will now reveal an advantage that arises from the greatness of your dominion. I think it has never yet occurred to you, and I never mentioned it in my previous speeches. It has so bold a sound that I should scarcely venture it now, were it not for the unnatural depression I see around me. You perhaps think that your empire extends only over your allies; I will tell you the truth. The visible field of action has two parts, land and sea. Over the whole of one of these you are completely supreme, not merely as far as you use it at present but to whatever further extent you think fit. In short, your naval resources are such that your vessels may go where they please, without the King or any other nation on earth being able to stop them. So although you may think it a great privation to lose the use of your land and houses, you must see that this power is something widely different. Instead of fretting over them, you should regard them as no more than the gardens and other embellishments of a great fortune, and as of little moment in comparison. You should know, too, that liberty preserved by your efforts will easily recover for us what we have lost, whereas once the knee is bowed, even what you have will pass from you. Your fathers received these possessions not from others but from themselves. They did not let slip what their labor had acquired, but handed it down safe to you; and in this respect at least you must prove yourselves their equals. Remember that to lose what one has got is more disgraceful than to be balked in getting it, and confront your enemies not merely with spirit but with disdain. A blissful ignorance can give confidence, even to a coward’s breast; but disdain is the privilege of those who, like us, have been assured by reflection of their superiority to their adversary. And where the chances are the same, knowledge fortifies courage through the contempt that follows from it. Its trust is placed not in hope, which is the prop of the desperate, but in a judgment grounded on existing resources, whose anticipations are more to be depended on.

“Again, your country has a right to your services in sustaining the glories of her position. These are a common source of pride to you all, and you cannot decline the burdens of empire and still expect to share its honors. You should remember also that you are fighting not merely against slavery in exchange for independence, but also against loss of empire and the danger arising from the animosities incurred in exercising it. Besides, it is no longer possible to draw back, if indeed any of you, in the alarm of the moment, has grown enamored of the honesty of such an unambitious part. For what you hold is, to speak somewhat plainly, a tyranny: to take it was perhaps wrong, but to let it go is unsafe. Men of these retiring views, if they made converts of others, would quickly ruin a state; and the result would be the same even if they could live independent by themselves. For the retiring and unambitious are never secure without vigorous protectors at their side. In short, such qualities are useless to an imperial city, though they may help a dependency to an unmolested servitude.

“But you must not be seduced by citizens like these, or be angry with me — who, if I voted for war, only did as you did yourselves. The enemy has invaded your country and done what you could be certain he would do if you refused to comply with his demands; and besides what we counted on, the plague has come upon us, the only point at which our calculation has been at fault. I know that this has had a large share in making me more unpopular than I should otherwise have been. That is quite undeserved, unless you are also prepared to give me the credit for any success that chance may bring you. Besides, the hand of heaven must be borne with resignation, that of the enemy with fortitude. This was the old way at Athens; do not now prevent it from being so still. Remember, too, that if your country has the greatest name in all the world, it is because she never bent before disaster. She has expended more life and effort in war than any other city, and has won for herself a power greater than any hitherto known, the memory of which will descend to the latest posterity. Even if now, in obedience to the general law of decay, we should ever be forced to yield, it will still be remembered that we held rule over more Hellenes than any other Hellenic state, that we sustained the greatest wars against their united or separate powers, and that we inhabited a city unrivalled by any other in resources or magnitude. These glories may incur the censure of the slow and unambitious; but in the breast of energy they will awaken emulation, and in those who must remain without them, an envious regret. Hatred and unpopularity at the moment have fallen to the lot of all who have aspired to rule others. But where odium must be incurred, true wisdom incurs it for the highest objects. Hatred, also, is short-lived; but what makes the splendor of the present and the glory of the future remains forever unforgotten. Make your decision, therefore, for glory hereafter and honor now, and attain both objects by instant and zealous effort. Do not send heralds to Lacedaemon, and do not betray any sign of being oppressed by your present sufferings. For the greatest men and the greatest communities are those whose minds are least sensitive to calamity and whose hands are quickest to meet it.”

Such were the arguments by which Pericles tried to cure the Athenians of their anger against him and to divert their thoughts from their immediate afflictions. As a community he succeeded in convincing them. They not only gave up all idea of sending to Lacedaemon but applied themselves with increased energy to the war. Still, as private individuals they could not help smarting under their sufferings. The common people had been deprived of the little they possessed, while the higher orders had lost fine properties, with costly establishments and buildings in the country, and, worst of all, had war instead of peace. In fact, the public feeling against him did not subside until he had been fined. Not long afterwards, however, as the multitude is wont to do, they elected him general again and committed all their affairs to his hands. They had by now become less sensitive to their private and domestic afflictions, and they understood that he was the best man of all for the public necessities. For as long as he was at the head of the state during the peace, he pursued a moderate and conservative policy, and in his time the state’s greatness was at its height. When the war broke out, here also he seems to have rightly gauged the power of his country. He outlived its commencement by two years and six months, and the correctness of his foresight about it became better known by his death. He told them to wait quietly, to pay attention to their navy, to attempt no new conquests, and to expose the city to no hazards during the war; if they did this, he promised them a favorable result. What they did was the very contrary. They let private ambitions and private interests, in matters apparently quite foreign to the war, lead them into projects unjust both to themselves and to their allies. The success of such projects would only bring honor and advantage to private persons, and their failure entailed certain disaster on the country in the war. The causes of this are not far to seek. Pericles, by his rank, his ability and his known integrity, was able to exercise an independent control over the multitude — in short, to lead them instead of being led by them. Because he never sought power by improper means, he was never compelled to flatter them; on the contrary, he enjoyed so high an estimation that he could afford to anger them by contradiction. Whenever he saw them unseasonably and insolently elated, he would reduce them to alarm with a word; and if they fell victim to a panic, he could at once restore them to confidence. In short, what was nominally a democracy became in his hands government by the first citizen. With his successors it was different. They were more on a level with one another, and each grasped at supremacy, so that they ended by committing even the conduct of state affairs to the whims of the multitude. This, as might have been expected in a great and sovereign state, produced a host of blunders, among them the Sicilian expedition. That expedition failed not so much through a miscalculation of the power of those against whom it was sent as through a fault in the senders. They did not take the best measures afterwards to assist those who had gone out, but chose rather to occupy themselves with private cabals for the leadership of the commons. By this they not only paralyzed operations in the field but also first introduced civil discord at home. Yet after losing most of their fleet in Sicily, besides other forces, and with faction already dominant in the city, they could still for three years make head against their original adversaries. These were joined not only by the Sicilians but by their own allies, nearly all in revolt, and at last by the King’s son, Cyrus, who furnished the funds for the Peloponnesian navy. Nor did the Athenians finally succumb until they fell victims to their own internal disorders. So superabundant were the resources from which the genius of Pericles foresaw an easy triumph in the war over the unaided forces of the Peloponnesians.

During the same summer the Lacedaemonians and their allies made an expedition with a hundred ships against Zacynthus, an island lying off the coast of Elis. It was peopled by a colony of Achaeans from Peloponnese and was in alliance with Athens. On board were a thousand Lacedaemonian heavy infantry, with Cnemus, a Spartan, as admiral. They landed from their ships and ravaged most of the country; but as the inhabitants would not submit, they sailed back home.

At the end of the same summer, the Corinthian Aristeus, Aneristus, Nicolaus and Stratodemus (envoys from Lacedaemon), Timagoras, a Tegean, and a private individual named Pollis from Argos were on their way to Asia to persuade the King to supply funds and join in the war. They came to Sitalces, son of Teres, in Thrace. They hoped to induce him, if possible, to abandon the alliance with Athens and march on Potidæa, then besieged by an Athenian force. They also wanted him to have them conveyed across the Hellespont to Pharnabazus, who was to send them up country to the King. But there happened to be with Sitalces some Athenian ambassadors, Learchus, son of Callimachus, and Ameiniades, son of Philemon. They persuaded Sitalces’ son Sadocus, the new Athenian citizen, to put the men into their hands, so as to prevent them from crossing over to the King and doing their part to injure the country of his choice. Sadocus accordingly had them seized as they were traveling through Thrace to the vessel in which they were to cross the Hellespont. The seizure was made by a party he had sent on with Learchus and Ameiniades, and he ordered the men delivered to the Athenian ambassadors, who brought them to Athens. On their arrival the Athenians were afraid that Aristeus, who had notably been the prime mover in the earlier affairs of Potidæa and their Thracian possessions, might live to do them still more mischief if he escaped. So they put them all to death the same day, without a trial and without hearing the defense that the men wished to offer, and cast their bodies into a pit. They thought themselves justified in retaliating with the same mode of warfare that the Lacedaemonians had begun, when they killed and cast into pits all the Athenian and allied traders whom they caught on board merchantmen around Peloponnese. Indeed, at the outset of the war the Lacedaemonians butchered as enemies all whom they took on the sea, whether allies of Athens or neutrals.

About the same time, toward the close of the summer, the Ambraciot forces, with a number of barbarians whom they had raised, marched against the Amphilochian Argos and the rest of that country. Their enmity against the Argives had the following origin. This Argos and the rest of Amphilochia were colonized by Amphilochus, son of Amphiaraus. He was dissatisfied with the state of affairs at home when he returned there after the Trojan War, so he built this city on the Ambracian Gulf and named it Argos after his own country. It was the largest town in Amphilochia, and its inhabitants were the most powerful. Many generations afterwards, pressed by misfortune, they called in the Ambraciots, their neighbors on the Amphilochian border, to join their colony. It was through this union with the Ambraciots that they learned their present Hellenic speech; the rest of the Amphilochians are barbarians. After a time the Ambraciots expelled the Argives and held the city themselves. Upon this the Amphilochians gave themselves over to the Acarnanians, and the two together called in the Athenians. The Athenians sent them Phormio as general and thirty ships; when these arrived, they took Argos by storm and made slaves of the Ambraciots, and the Amphilochians and Acarnanians inhabited the town in common. After this began the alliance between the Athenians and Acarnanians. The enmity of the Ambraciots against the Argives thus began with the enslavement of their citizens. Afterwards, during the war, they gathered this armament from among themselves, the Chaonians and other neighboring barbarians. They arrived before Argos and became masters of the country, but they were unsuccessful in their attacks on the town, and returned home and dispersed among their different peoples.

Such were the events of the summer. The following winter the Athenians sent twenty ships around Peloponnese under the command of Phormio, who stationed himself at Naupactus and kept watch against anyone sailing in or out of Corinth and the Crissaean Gulf. Six others went to Caria and Lycia under Melesander, to collect tribute in those parts and also to prevent the Peloponnesian privateers from taking up a station in those waters and molesting the passage of merchantmen from Phaselis, Phoenicia and the adjoining continent. However, Melesander went up the country into Lycia with a force of Athenians from the ships and of the allies, and was defeated and killed in battle, with the loss of a number of his troops.

The same winter the Potidæans at length found they could no longer hold out against their besiegers. The inroads of the Peloponnesians into Attica had not had the desired effect of making the Athenians raise the siege. No provisions were left, and distress for food in Potidæa had gone so far that, besides a number of other horrors, there had even been instances of the people eating one another. In this extremity they at last made proposals for capitulating to the Athenian generals in command against them: Xenophon, son of Euripides, Hestiodorus, son of Aristocleides, and Phanomachus, son of Callimachus. The generals accepted, seeing the sufferings of the army in so exposed a position, and since the state had already spent two thousand talents on the siege. The terms of the capitulation were as follows: a free passage out for the Potidæans, their children, wives and auxiliaries, with one garment apiece, and two for the women, and a fixed sum of money for their journey. Under this treaty they went out to Chalcidice and other places, as each was able. The Athenians, however, blamed the generals for granting terms without instructions from home, since they were of the opinion that the place would have had to surrender at discretion. Afterwards they sent settlers of their own to Potidæa and colonized it. Such were the events of the winter, and so ended the second year of this war of which Thucydides was the historian.
